description: Hand-verified transient-failure classifier corpus harvested from past dogfood sessions (dogfood-38). Each entry maps real error text to the expected is_transient_failure() verdict; expectations are ground truth fixed by the mission author.
harvest_note: Strings collected by scanning .tether/sessions/*/report.json, responses/*.json and verification/*.json across all 24 sessions present at harvest time. No transient_retry event was ever recorded in these sessions: the dogfood-33/34 provider flake was captured with the flake text in logs while error was 'exit code 1', so it is encoded both as surfaced adapter error (transient, per dogfood-34 signatures) and as captured (fatal, per the never-scan-logs contract).

entries.error: Error from provider (Console): Upstream request failed: Endpoint is unavailable.
entries.justification: Real provider upstream outage text observed live while Tether dogfooded itself; matched case-insensitively by the 'upstream request failed' / 'endpoint is unavailable' signatures added in dogfood-34.

entries.logs: [91m[1mError: [0mError from provider (Console): Upstream request failed: Endpoint is unavailable.
entries.justification: As actually captured: flake text lived in logs and error was only 'exit code 1'. The classifier deliberately never scans logs (agent/test output legitimately mentions outage words), so this genuine-looking state must not retry - pinning that historical no-retry behavior.
Tether's own agent-timeout kill from adapters/command.py; generic timeout wording stays non-transient so timeouts drive recovery exactly once instead of burning retries.
Same class as the 1800s kill: Tether's own timeout semantics are genuine failures, never retried as infrastructure flakes.
Verification command killed by SIGTERM after its deadline (negative returncode -15); timeout kills are a genuine failure class owned by the recovery loop, not an infrastructure flake.
Ordinary agent mistake: a real assertion failure from dogfood-32's first verification attempt; recovered via repair, never via retry.
Ordinary agent mistake: failing test assertion captured verbatim from a real verification run; must drive repair, not retry.

entries.source: representative of ordinary agent mistakes (no verbatim SyntaxError survived in session artifacts)
entries.justification: Agent-authored code defect class required by the mission corpus; pure code mistake, always repaired never retried.
The single most common real failure signature in the audit trail: adapter CLI exited nonzero for ordinary reasons; nothing infrastructure-flake-shaped, so no retry.

entries.source: derived from real outcomes: dogfood-30/33 review sends whose verdict parse found no output ('no valid review verdict found in reviewer output')
entries.justification: Empty-output failure: agent produced zero output on a send; absence of any flake signature must keep prior fail-safe semantics (recovery/fail-closed), not retry.

near_misses.justification: Signature word alone without the outage phrase must never match.
Shares words with 'upstream request failed' but is an application-level validation error.

near_misses.error: endpoint returned HTTP 500 with validation traceback
near_misses.justification: Adjacent status code 500 is deliberately not a gateway-flake signature (only 502/503/504 are).

near_misses.logs: print('Upstream Request Failed: Endpoint is unavailable.')
near_misses.justification: Agent-authored code printing provider-like text into its own output: logs are never scanned, so this stays fatal.
Word-boundary guard: embedded 502-like digit runs inside larger numbers must not match.
Trailing digits defeat the \b boundary: 50300 is data, not a gateway status.
Provider/console vocabulary alone carries no verdict weight without an exact signature phrase.

near_misses.logs: network_error overload 503 handled gracefully by retry helper under test
near_misses.justification: Completed states are never transient regardless of what their captured output mentions.
No text at all: nothing can match, state keeps plain non-transient semantics.
